summary: The Netnews Administration System is an experimental framework to simplify administration and use of Usenet. Data about newsgroups and hierarchies sit in a distributed hierarchical database reachable by a client-server protocol, used by news servers, administrators and readers, and it coexists with existing control messages.

eli5.summary: Usenet has many discussion boards with messy rules. This experiment proposes a shared, organized directory describing them so servers and readers can look things up.

questions: what is the netnews administration system
how does nas differ from usenet control messages
what is a nas protocol level
subtitle: An experimental directory service telling news servers, admins and readers which Usenet newsgroups and hierarchies exist and their state.

tldr.problem: Usenet administration relied on old tools and on control messages that are often faked, so many hierarchies are inconsistent, new groups are created late and dead groups linger.
tldr.mechanism: NAS keeps newsgroup and hierarchy data in a distributed hierarchical database that clients query over a text-based, NNTP- and SMTP-style protocol on TCP port 991, with signed server-to-server transfers.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document with an IESG note saying the IETF disclaims any knowledge of its fitness and that readers should be cautious. Its UDP part was left to a separate paper.

today: RFC 4707 is an Experimental document, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its IESG note says it is not a candidate for any Internet Standard and urges caution about implementing or deploying it.

sections.title: The Problem NAS Addresses
sections.content:
The Netnews Administration System (NAS) is a framework to simplify the administration and use of network news. The RFC says the growing numbers of newsgroups, hierarchies and articles made server administration complex, while the tools had stayed unchanged for ten years.

It lists several symptoms: inconsistent hierarchies, new groups created late or never, removed groups lingering in configuration files, and users who cannot easily find a group's charter, preferred language or whether it is moderated. Faked control messages are a further problem, so many servers disable automatic group creation and removal, leaving dead groups in place.

NAS is an out-of-band system. It does not use control messages or special NNTP commands, so there is no interference with current protocols, and it carries more structured information than a control message.

The RFC carries an IESG note: it is not a candidate for any Internet Standard, was not published after IETF review of security or interaction with deployed protocols, and readers should exercise caution when evaluating it for implementation and deployment.
sections.eli5: Right now, lists of message boards go stale and people sometimes send fake notes saying a board was added or removed. NAS gives everyone one trustworthy place to ask.

sections.title: A Hierarchy of NAS Servers
sections.content:
NAS is comparable to directory services such as DNS, LDAP or NIS. The database is hierarchical and distributed: a root server collects data from sub-servers that are authoritative for particular hierarchies, signs it and distributes it. Servers can be non-authoritative, merely passing on what they collected. Replication is possible and the structure can have multiple levels.

Clients are news servers (which can update their configuration automatically), administrators (who fetch data manually) and news reader programs (which can show users details about groups and hierarchies). An attached timestamp distinguishes new from old data and avoids loops in propagation.

The RFC accepts that policy problems may arise with a single root. At startup a root might handle only hierarchies with strict rules and accepted authorities, and other servers could serve other sets such as alt.*. An administrator can use one root server or choose another server for particular hierarchies. A request goes through connection, optional authentication, optional protocol level negotiation, queries and termination.
sections.eli5: It works like a chain of librarians. Each librarian knows one shelf well, a head librarian collects all the lists, and anyone can ask any librarian, who may have gotten the answer from another.

sections.title: Protocol Levels
sections.content:
Because the protocol is expected to change, NAS has a protocol level, a number between 1 and 32767 negotiated at connection setup. This document describes level 1. Every implementation MUST be compatible with level 1 so it can fall back if a higher level fails, and enhancements MUST use a different level and state how they behave at other levels.

The client uses VERS to ask for a level and the server replies with the highest it accepts, never higher than requested. If nothing is negotiated, level 1 is used.
sections.eli5: It is like two people agreeing on which edition of a rule book to use. If they cannot agree on a newer one, they use edition 1, which everybody has.

sections.title: Commands and Responses
sections.content:
NAS uses TCP, typically on port 991. On connection the server immediately sends a greeting beginning with code 200. It refuses with 434 if the client has no permission (decided from its IP address) or 404 when out of service, then closes the connection.

Commands are case-insensitive, four-character words, optionally followed by parameters. Answers begin with a three-digit response code, then text lines ended by CRLF, and a line holding a single period marks the end. A line starting with a period has it doubled. The first digit of a code gives the type (1xx information, 2xx success, 3xx success with data, 4xx accepted but no operation possible, 5xx wrong or unimplemented request, 6xx success with data until the end mark). The second digit gives the category, such as connection (x0x), queries (x1x) or server-server communication (x2x).

The query commands are LIST (groups and sub-hierarchies directly under a hierarchy, with status), LSTR (a recursive list that accepts a trailing star wildcard), HIER (all information on a hierarchy) and DATA (information on a newsgroup). GETP and GETA are for server-server use: both send a timestamp so the server can answer that the client's copy is current (213 or 215), or return the data. With timestamp 0 the data is always sent. Syntax is defined in ABNF.
sections.eli5: You type short four-letter requests like LIST, and the server answers with a number telling you how it went, then the details, ending with a single dot on its own line.

sections.title: Status Values and Data Headers
sections.content:
Each hierarchy or newsgroup has a status. Hierarchies can be Complete, Incomplete, Obsolete or Unknown. Newsgroups can be Unmoderated, Readonly, Moderated, Removed or Unknown. Newsgroup types include Discussion, Binary, Sources, Announce, Test, Robots and Experiment. Hierarchy types include Global, Regional, Alt, Non-commercial, Commercial and Organization.

Answers to HIER and DATA are blocks of headers. Name starts a new block and Status is always given. Optional headers include Serial, Followup, Description, Charter, Netiquette, FAQ, Rules and control or moderator details such as Ctl-Send-Adr and Mod-Sub-Adr. A group's control or moderator PGP key can also be returned.
sections.eli5: Each board has a label saying whether it is open, closed, moderated or deleted, plus an information card with its rules and who to contact.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
At protocol level 1, security is addressed only for server-server communication. The username and password in GETA and GETP limit connections to authorised clients, and NAS data is signed with PGP keys according to RFC 2440 so that it can be verified as authentic and untampered. A server may also deny commands or the whole connection by the client's IP number.

No mechanism lets a client check that it is talking to a legitimate server or that the data it receives is authentic. The RFC says a stronger authentication scheme will come in a higher protocol level.
sections.eli5: Servers swapping lists with each other use passwords and signed envelopes. A reader, however, cannot yet check that the answer really came from the right server.
